lead: A turbocharger is a turbine driven by exhaust gas that spins a compressor and pushes more air into the engine. The exhaust energy is otherwise wasted. The catch is time: the rotor has mass and takes a moment to speed up, and that delay is turbo lag. Turbochargers are common on small petrol and diesel cars, tractors and trucks, where more air means more fuel burnt and more power from a smaller engine.
prereq: You need: Supercharging for pressure ratio, delivery temperature and density ratio.

sections.h3: Layout and the two turbocharging methods

blocks.text: A turbocharger has a turbine wheel and a compressor wheel on one shaft, held in an oil-fed bearing housing. Exhaust gas drives the turbine wheel; the shaft spins the compressor wheel, which draws air through the air filter and pushes it into the intake manifold at higher pressure and density. A wastegate valve lets some exhaust bypass the turbine, and its actuator sets the boost.
The energy comes from exhaust enthalpy, which the turbine extracts as the gas cools and expands; a turbocharger is an exhaust-driven supercharger.

Two manifold methods are common. In constant-pressure turbocharging, all cylinders feed one exhaust manifold. The pulses mix and the turbine sees an almost steady pressure. This suits steady high-load running, but at low load response is slow. In pulse turbocharging, narrow pipes keep the exhaust pulses separate and aim them at the turbine. Boost builds earlier, so most road vehicles use pulse turbocharging.

A single turbo must work from low to rated speed, so its size is a compromise. Twin turbos can be parallel: two small, quick-spooling turbos, each fed by half the cylinders. Twin turbos can also be in series: a small turbo makes boost at low speed, a large turbo takes over at high speed, and valves switch the flow. A crank-driven blower, covered in Supercharging, gives boost as soon as the engine turns, but it takes power from the crankshaft.

sections.h3: Boost threshold is not turbo lag

blocks.text: Boost threshold is the lowest engine speed, at a given load, where the exhaust flow can spin the turbine fast enough for the compressor to exceed atmospheric pressure. Below the threshold the turbo is a restriction, not a boost source. A large turbine housing raises the threshold; a small one lowers it. The threshold is a speed.

Turbo lag is a time. Open the throttle at a speed above the threshold and the boost does not appear at once. The exhaust gas must first accelerate the turbine wheel, shaft and compressor wheel; the intake pipes and intercooler must then fill with denser air. A typical small petrol turbo takes about one to two seconds to reach full boost after a throttle step. The rotor stores kinetic energy ½Jω², where J is its moment of inertia in kg·m² and ω its speed in rad/s, and the turbine can only supply that energy at the rate its surplus power allows. The figure plots the second worked example: the rotor climbs from 30 000 to 150 000 rev/min in about 1.3 s.

Lag is felt as a pause followed by a surge, worst after a gear change or a spell of light-load cruising. The cure is not more boost; it is less rotating mass, a smaller turbine housing, or split exhaust pulses.

Matching a turbocharger means choosing a compressor and turbine that work well together over the engine range. On the compressor side, the operating point at cruise should sit inside the high-efficiency island, typically 70 to 75 percent, away from surge at low flow and choke at high flow. On the turbine side, the shaft speed must stay below its limit at rated power. A wastegate protects the turbine: when boost reaches the set value, the actuator opens the wastegate and bypasses exhaust around the turbine. Less exhaust through the turbine means less turbine power, so boost stops rising.

Lag-reduction hardware attacks inertia and exhaust volume. A small turbine housing raises gas velocity at low flow, at the cost of exhaust backpressure at high flow. A twin-scroll turbine housing keeps the pulses from cylinders that would otherwise interfere; Lightweight turbine and compressor wheels, and ball bearings instead of journal bearings, cut the rotating mass and friction. Variable geometry, covered in Variable geometry turbochargers and intercooling, changes the turbine nozzle area with speed. The term anti-lag system (ALS) means something else: a rally-car trick that retards the spark and burns fuel in the exhaust manifold to keep the turbine spinning when the driver lifts off. Road cars do not use it.

The bearing housing gets pressurised oil from the engine; the film supports the shaft and carries heat away from the hot turbine end. After a hard run the turbine housing is very hot. If the engine stops at once, oil flow stops and the oil left in the bearing housing can cook into carbon, damaging the bearing and seal; this is heat soak. Idling for a minute or two lets oil carry the heat away. Water-cooled bearing housings reduce the risk.

figure.caption: The second worked example as a curve: with 1.8 kW of surplus turbine power, the rotor takes 1.32 s to climb from 30 000 to 150 000 rev/min. A rotor with 30 per cent less inertia gets there in 0.92 s.

spec.aria: Rotor speed in thousands of revolutions per minute against time from 0 to 1.6 seconds. Two rising curves start at 30 thousand; the heavier rotor reaches 150 thousand at 1.32 seconds, the lighter one at 0.92 seconds.

examples.question: A 2 litre turbocharged petrol engine at 3000 rev/min draws 0.080 kg/s of air through its compressor. The compressor takes air at 300 K and 1.0 bar, has pressure ratio 1.6 and isentropic efficiency 0.70 (γ = 1.4, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K). The engine runs at an air-fuel ratio of 14.7. For the exhaust gas take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.15 kJ/kg·K; the turbo shaft and bearings have a mechanical efficiency of 0.95. Find the compressor power, the turbine power and the temperature drop of the exhaust across the turbine.
steps: Compressor delivery temperature, as for a supercharger: T₂ₛ = 300 × 1.6<sup>0.286</sup> = 343.1 K, and T₂ = 300 + 43.1/0.70 = 361.6 K. Temperature rise ΔT<sub>a</sub> = 61.6 K.
Compressor power P<sub>c</sub> = ṁ<sub>a</sub> c<sub>p,a</sub> ΔT<sub>a</sub> = 0.080 × 1.005 × 61.6 = 4.95 kW.
The turbine must also cover the bearing friction: P<sub>t</sub> = P<sub>c</sub> ÷ η<sub>m</sub> = 4.95 ÷ 0.95 = 5.21 kW.
Exhaust mass flow is air plus fuel: fuel = 0.080 ÷ 14.7 = 0.0054 kg/s, so ṁ<sub>g</sub> = 0.0854 kg/s.
Turbine power is also ṁ<sub>g</sub> c<sub>p,g</sub> ΔT<sub>t</sub>, so ΔT<sub>t</sub> = 5.21 ÷ (0.0854 × 1.15) = 5.21 ÷ 0.0982 = 53.1 K.
examples.answer: Compressor power 4.95 kW, turbine power 5.21 kW, and the exhaust cools by about 53 K across the turbine: energy that a naturally aspirated engine throws away.

examples.question: A small turbo rotor (turbine wheel, shaft and compressor wheel) has a moment of inertia J = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg·m². At a throttle step it must spin up from 30 000 to 150 000 rev/min, and the turbine has, on average, 1.8 kW more power than the compressor and bearings absorb. Estimate the lag. How much shorter is it with a lighter rotor of 30 percent less inertia?
steps: Convert speeds: ω₁ = 30 000 × 2π/60 = 3142 rad/s; ω₂ = 150 000 × 2π/60 = 15 708 rad/s.
Time at 1800 W of surplus power: t = ΔE ÷ P = 2369 ÷ 1800 = 1.32 s.
With J reduced by 30 percent, ΔE and t fall by 30 percent: t = 0.7 × 1.32 = 0.92 s.
examples.answer: About 1.3 s of lag; a 30 percent lighter rotor cuts it to about 0.9 s, which is why light wheels and ball bearings matter.

traps: Lag and boost threshold get mixed up. Threshold is a speed below which no boost is possible; lag is a time delay at a speed where boost is possible.
The wastegate bypasses exhaust around the turbine. It does not dump intake air, and it does not open the compressor side.
A large turbine housing lowers exhaust backpressure at high power but raises the boost threshold. A small housing spools quickly but can choke the top end.
Boost is often given in bar gauge while pressure ratio is absolute. At sea level, 1.0 bar gauge means pressure ratio about 2.0, not 1.0.

quiz.q: Name the main parts of a turbocharger and state the function of the bearing housing.
quiz.a: Turbine wheel and housing, compressor wheel and housing, shaft, bearing housing, wastegate and actuator. The bearing housing holds the shaft in an oil film and carries heat away from the turbine end.

quiz.q: Why does pulse turbocharging give better low-speed response than constant-pressure turbocharging?
quiz.a: Pulse turbocharging keeps the exhaust pulses apart in narrow pipes and aims them at the turbine, so their energy arrives quickly. Constant-pressure turbocharging mixes all pulses in one large manifold, so at low load the turbine sees a steadier, weaker flow and responds slowly.

quiz.q: A turbocharger gives 0.8 bar gauge boost at sea level where atmospheric pressure is 1.0 bar. Find the compressor pressure ratio.
quiz.a: Absolute outlet pressure = 1.0 + 0.8 = 1.8 bar. Pressure ratio = 1.8 / 1.0 = 1.8.

quiz.q: A driver says the car has no power below 1800 rpm but pulls strongly after 2000 rpm. Is this lag or boost threshold? Explain.
quiz.a: Mainly the boost threshold. Below about 1800 rev/min the exhaust cannot spin the turbine fast enough to make boost at all. Lag is the delay after a throttle step at a speed above that.

quiz.q: A wastegate actuator is stuck closed. What happens at high engine speed and load?
quiz.a: No exhaust can bypass the turbine, so turbine speed and boost keep rising past the set value. The charge gets very hot, the engine may knock or overload, and the turbo can overspeed and fail.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to idle for a minute before switching off a hot turbocharged engine?
quiz.a: Idling keeps oil flowing through the bearing housing while the turbine housing cools slightly. If the engine stops at once, oil trapped in the hot bearing housing can cook into carbon and damage the bearing and seal.

quiz.q: How does a twin-scroll turbine housing reduce turbo lag?
quiz.a: It keeps apart the exhaust of cylinders whose pulses would interfere. Each pulse reaches the turbine wheel with more energy and less mixing, so the wheel spins up faster at low speed.

beyond: Production engines increasingly use an electric motor on the turbo shaft, or a separate electric compressor, to make boost before exhaust energy arrives. Search next for turbocharger matching, compressor map, twin-scroll turbine and electric turbocharger.
